Benedicto reyes Cabrera (born April 10, 1942), better known as "BenCab", is a Filipino painter who was conferred a National Artist of the Philippines for Visual Arts (Painting) in 2006. He has been noted as "arguably the best-selling painter of his generation of Filipino artists."

Early life and education

BenCab was born to Democrito Cabrera and Isabel Reyes in Malabon, Philippines on April 10, 1942. He was the youngest of nine children. BenCab's first exposure and discovery of the arts happened through his elder brother, Salvador, who was already an established artist during Bencab's childhood. 

He went on to study at the University of the Philippines Diliman. He received his bachelor's degree in Fine Arts in 1963.

Family and European career

BenCab met British journalist Caroline Kennedy (author of An Affair of State, 1987, and How the English Establishment Framed Stephen Ward, 2013) in Manila in 1968, and married her in London in 1969. The couple decided to stay in London. They have three children. The eldest, Elisar (b. 1971; d. 2020), a film and web series producer, was married to award-winning playwright and web series writer, Lisa Gifford. Their middle child, Mayumi, was born in Manila in 1973 and became a successful model both in London and Los Angeles. She currently lives in Los Angeles with her partner, John A. For Dannie Zhang, it's all about the power to choose, to change and to be yourself at any given moment.

That's why, even though she was raised since age 12 to be a Chinese opera actress – face painted, sword in hand, flipping kung-fu style as a lady fighter – she up and quit one day after seven years on the stage and moved to the United States.

That's why, although fate led to love in China, she created a life to suit her love of America.

And that's why her grand plan gives her children their choice of careers in either country, even though right now it leaves one son at Fairmont Private School in Anaheim and one son with her husband, thousands of miles away.

The wrist-flick she perfected for swordplay in Shandong Province has since been used for wrapping dumplings in San Gabriel and wielding curling irons in Rosemead.

The next step in her path may bring the lady fighter back to her homeland with a few American flourishes.

• • •

If you're going to master the singing, dancing, acting and kung-fu fighting of traditional Chinese opera, you have to start young.

Zhang was 12 when she was selected for the arts academy. It wasn't long before her role was decided: She wouldn't be the flirt, the lover or the wise woman. She'd be the warrior.

She could take a hit and roll to the ground or kung-fu flip and sword-slice the air as well as the boys.

In the early years, performances were packed. But as movies became more accessible, opera audiences waned.

As she approached her mid-20s, Zhang dreamed of learning a new skill and starting fresh. But it seemed impossible to her.

"If I stay in China, it is really hard to really leave my work," Zhang says. "So many friends, co-workers and family, they will stop you."

Some television show creators believe in the division of labor. Others believe in the age-old age that if you want something done well, you'd rather do it yourself. There are therefore several shows where the person who came up with the idea is also a regular cast member. In most cases, the multitaskers tend to be people whose resume already has an acting gig or two. They are familiar with what it takes to give a good performance and aren't just taking multiple roles because it's their project.

By serving as both creators and actors, these individuals get to do what they love the most while steering things from within. Because of this approach, any on-set proceedings that don't align with their vision can easily be rectified. Consequently, many shows that fall under this category tend to be critically acclaimed award magnets.

15 Tina Fey in 30 Rock (2006 – 2013)

30 Rock is a comical look into what life is like for the people who work behind the scenes during the production of a sketch comedy series. Tina Fey plays the TGS head writer Liz Lemon, and she does it all effortlessly because she once served as a writer for Saturday Night Live. The role earned her Emmy nominations for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series five years in a row. Hers is a rare case where the role she plays in the fictional universe is the same one she plays behind the scenes. When I told my husband what the topic of this week's rec list was, he was like, "shouldn't we be discouraging that type of relationship?" Well, yes, if romance books were the real world. There's generally an inherent sense of "wrongness" to boss/employee romances, which is one of the staples of the trope. The characters KNOW it's a terrible idea that is likely to end badly, and that adds a level of tension. Romance authors often build in a workaround so that the situation isn't so cut and dry – maybe the heroine actually reports to someone else, maybe it's just a temporary situation, maybe they don't cross the line until something shifts. But the forbidden element is certainly all part of the story.

What I love about grumpy boss rom coms is the long-term forced proximity; these characters see each other every day, and they have no choice but to deal with the situation. Sometimes the tension between them crackles from the minute they meet, sometimes it snaps after years of buildup. The journey is always interesting though, and a grumpy boss tends to fall in love while kicking and screaming. Metaphorically, of course – it's probably more like smirking and growling, in actuality. Either way, the ride is always a lot of fun, and the perfect environment for tons of sexual tension. Add in the com part of these roms, and grumpy boss romances have all the makings of a great read… which is probably why we're all so willing to overlook the real world impracticalities.

Every book on this list has its own unique vibe and scenario. From super spicy to closed door, there's a little something for everyone on this list. It's never easy to say goodbye, even if it's a television goodbye. While no TV show can last forever – well, Law & Order: SVU is in the running – the cast doesn't always stay as long. Many actors choose to leave after their contracts end. Some give the networks a lengthy heads-up, while others just seem to up and vanish, leaving the writers to scramble (see below!). Regardless, the show must go on.

One of the most talked about exits was in May 2017, when Sophia Bush decided to leave Chicago P.D. after season 4. She played the lead role of Detective Erin Lindsay on the NBC drama and was written out of the show with a cliffhanger – her character was offered a job in New York to join the FBI. Many thought this could mean she would pop up on Law & Order: SVU – another show written by Dick Wolf which has done a crossover with P.D. before – but over the years, it was made apparent that was not happening.

In multiple interviews since her exit, Bush explained that she went to her bosses between the third and fourth seasons and told them if things didn't "drastically" change, she would be leaving at the end of the year. Then, in December 2018, she opened up about the decision while on Dax Shepard's "Armchair Expert" podcast.

"I quit because, what I've learned is, I've been so programmed to be a good girl and to be a work horse and be a tug boat, that I have always prioritized tugging the ship for the crew, for the show, for the group, ahead of my own health … My body was, like, falling apart, because I was really, really unhappy," she revealed, before later adding she felt "ignored" and recalled the time she told a coworker, "I feel like I was standing butt-naked, bruised and bleeding in the middle of Times Square, screaming at the top of my lungs and not a single person stopped to ask if they could help me."

"You should be here!!!" my colleague emphatically messages me. "I'm in a meeting and you should so hear what this guy is saying."

"Hey!!" texts a second colleague. "Where are you? This speaker is talking about our event. He loves us!"

Yes, I should be at that meeting.

It's not that I'm avoiding work or didn't feel like attending said meeting. I missed this soiree and about 1,000 impromptu water cooler conversations, sidebar rants, and in-person events every week. As a remote employee, I was in my home office at the time of this particular presentation. I was 2,277 miles away.

But not to worry. My work sister wives had my back. Within minutes of the first text, we'd hatched a plan—Work Sister Wife One would take a video of the presentation and Work Sister Wife Two would introduce herself to the speaker and pass along my information. As always, I was covered by girl proxy.

A work sister wife. To be fair, I'm taking liberties with terminology. A sister wife, by actual definition, is a controversial relationship where a woman is both sister and wife; a co-wife to the same husband. My workplace definition, on the other hand, is less likely to get you scrutinized by neighbors, colleagues, and law enforcement in 49.5 states.

Work sister wife, or husband: (noun) a person who is simultaneously a confidante, coworker, and proxy; a trusted friend who acts as a professional stand-in during meetings and presentations; an in-person voice to your virtual opinions; a decision-making delegate upon your behalf.

I'm intentionally leaving out the polyamory component of this equation, although one could argue that most people engage in a polyamorous relationship with their company. In the words of many, professional monogamy is dying out. The gig is on, so to speak.
